items.text: Every sport skill rides on top of one engine, how much force a kid puts into the ground, how fast, how explosively. A great swing or a sharp cut still has to be powered by something.
Think of your athlete like a car. The sport-specific drills... that's the paint job and the trim. It matters. But none of it moves the car.
items.notes: Engine/paint intuition pump (constructed framing device, NOT brand IP)

items.text: The engine is the athletic part. How much force the kid puts into the ground, how fast, how explosively.
Most families spend everything on paint and never touch the engine.
items.notes: Neglected-engine claim; Medium B: 'The mechanics were never the problem. The engine was.'

items.text: A bigger engine is a first step that beats the defender to the ball, which turns into more plays made, until the kid who used to get there a beat late is the one arriving first.
first step that beats the defender to the ball, which turns into more plays made every game, which becomes the kind of tape a coach stops to watch, until the kid... is the one getting there first.
A perfectly coached skill on top of a weak engine still loses the race to the ball... the skill got sharper but the engine never changed.
You can't coach a kid into more force production with a clipboard, the same way you can't paint a car into going faster. Those are two different jobs, and almost nobody is doing the second one.
items.notes: Long A — reconciles skill coaching vs engine building

items.text: This isn't a knock on skill coaching, by the way. Skill work matters, and a kid needs it.
